meta.subtitle: AIDC leader raises its 2026 outlook, but tariff and currency tailwinds are transitory and the shares sit near a 52-week high.

analystSentiment.commentary: Coverage is constructive but not unanimous: of 16 analysts, 10 rate Zebra Buy, 6 Hold and none Sell, for a consensus Buy. The consensus price target is $411.45, about 11.9% above the current $367.54, with a median of $420.00 and a range of $350.00 to $455.00. The Street's optimism rests on the raised full-year outlook and the gross-margin expansion shown this quarter. Our reading is more cautious: much of the reported upside is transitory, organic growth is high-single-digit, and the shares already sit below the Street's consensus and median targets, so even allowing for that we land one notch below at HOLD.

executiveSummary.companyOverview: Zebra Technologies Corporation is a global leader in the Automatic Identification and Data Capture ('AIDC') industry, which spans mobile computing, barcode scanning and imaging, RFID, thermal barcode printing and related supplies, real-time location systems and workflow software. The company was founded in 1969 and is headquartered in Lincolnshire, Illinois. It sells through a direct sales force and a network of channel partners into retail and e-commerce, manufacturing, transportation and logistics, healthcare and the public sector. As of the quarter ended July 4, 2026, Zebra reports in two segments: Connected Frontline ('CF'), which brings together mobile computing, point-of-sale, self-service kiosks and workflow software, and Asset Visibility & Automation ('AVA'), which covers thermal printing and supplies, data capture, fixed industrial scanning, machine vision, RFID and real-time location systems. On September 30, 2025 the company acquired Elo Holdings, Inc. ('Elo') for approximately $1.3 billion, adding to the Connected Frontline segment.

thesis.label: HOLD
thesis.body: Zebra is a quality AIDC franchise whose reported results are running ahead of its underlying demand. Net sales in the quarter ended July 4, 2026 rose {+ 20.4% +} to $1,557 million and gross margin expanded {+ 540 bps +} to 53.0%, but the margin gain leaned on roughly $73 million of IEEPA import-tariff recoveries and favorable foreign currency, and organic net sales grew a more modest 9.2%. About 8 points of guided full-year growth come from acquisitions, dispositions and currency rather than the base business. At $367.54, near the top of a 52-week range of $199.05 to $386.23, the stock trades at about 17.5x forward earnings. That is a fair multiple for a mid-single-digit organic grower, but it leaves little room for error if the enterprise-hardware cycle turns, as it did in FY23.

catalysts: Raised outlook: management lifted its full-year 2026 sales-growth, margin and free-cash-flow targets.
Margin momentum: adjusted EBITDA margin reached 27.7% in the quarter and is guided to 23.5% to 24.0% for the full year.
Elo integration: the $1.3 billion Elo acquisition adds scale to the Connected Frontline segment.
Automation demand: management ties growth to automation and 'Physical AI' adoption across frontline operations.
Capital return: the company keeps returning cash through buybacks and pays no dividend.
risks: Transitory tailwinds: tariff recoveries and favorable currency lifted quarterly margins and will not recur at that scale.
Cyclicality: AIDC hardware demand tracks enterprise capital spending, which turned down in FY23.
Inorganic mix: roughly 8 points of guided full-year growth come from acquisitions and currency, not organic demand.
Leverage: total debt reached $2,776 million as of July 4, 2026 after the Elo deal, and the current ratio is 0.52.
Valuation: near a 52-week high, the shares already discount continued execution.

income.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December (52/53-week fiscal year).

financials.incomeCommentary: Net sales in the quarter ended July 4, 2026 were $1,557 million, {+ up 20.4% +} from $1,293 million a year earlier, with growth in both segments and across all regions. The page snapshot renders the same quarter as about +18% and labels it Q3'26, reflecting a calendar-quarter mapping; we use the filing's own second-quarter figures throughout. Tangible product sales led at $1,316 million, {+ up 24.7% +}, while services and software were $241 million. Gross margin rose to 53.0% from 47.6%, an increase of {+ 540 bps +}, which management attributes primarily to IEEPA tariff recoveries and favorable foreign currency; adjusted gross margin was 53.3%. Operating income was $321 million, {+ up 75.4% +} from $183 million, and diluted EPS was $4.85 versus $2.19. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $6.35 against $3.61. The headline overstates the trend: consolidated organic net sales, which strip out currency and the Elo acquisition, grew 9.2% in the quarter and 6.8% year to date. The longer record is uneven — revenue fell {- -20.7% -} in FY23 before recovering to $5.4B in FY25 at an 8.3% growth rate — a reminder that this is a cyclical enterprise-hardware business rather than a steady compounder.

balance.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December (52/53-week fiscal year).

financials.balanceCommentary: As of July 4, 2026, Zebra held cash and cash equivalents of $157 million against total debt of $2,776 million, so the balance sheet carries meaningful net leverage. Debt has climbed from $2.5B at the FY25 year-end, reflecting the September 30, 2025 Elo acquisition for approximately $1.3 billion, and management notes higher interest expense on higher average debt balances. FY25 net debt was $2.4B against total equity of $3.6B. Liquidity is thin on the current ratio, which stood at 0.52 on a trailing basis and has been below 1.0 in three of the last five fiscal years, so the company relies on its cash generation and revolving capacity rather than a large cash cushion. The Elo deal also added goodwill and intangibles that the FY2025 Form 10-K identifies as at risk of impairment if the acquired business underperforms.

cashflow.note: Source: Bigdata.com company tearsheet (FMP); fiscal years ended December (52/53-week fiscal year).

financials.cashflowCommentary: Cash generation is the strongest part of the story. Over the six months ended July 4, 2026, operating cash flow was $387 million and capital expenditure just $26 million, leaving free cash flow of $361 million. The model is capital-light — FY25 capital expenditure was $86 million, under 2% of sales — and FY25 free cash flow was $831M. Cash returns run entirely through buybacks rather than a dividend, funded by that free cash flow. The cash line is not immune to the cycle: operating cash flow fell to roughly break-even in FY23 and free cash flow that year was negative, so the guided full-year figure assumes the current demand environment holds.

multiples.note: Peer multiples pending a peer data source.

valuation.multiplesCommentary: On trailing GAAP earnings the stock looks expensive at 33.6x, but that multiple is distorted by a depressed earnings base — diluted EPS was $8.18 in FY25 after a weaker prior stretch. The forward picture is more reasonable: shares trade at about 17.5x next-twelve-month earnings and roughly 16.6x FY27 consensus EPS of $22.20, with price-to-sales at 3.0x; an EV/EBITDA multiple is not available in the pack. Wall Street's price targets sit modestly above the current price. The forward multiple is defensible for a business guiding low-double-digit total and mid-single-digit organic growth, but it does not embed a margin reset if the tariff and currency tailwinds fade or the hardware cycle softens.

scenarios.name: Bull
scenarios.driver: Automation and 'Physical AI' demand broadens, organic growth re-accelerates into double digits, Elo proves accretive, and adjusted EBITDA margin holds near the top of the 23.5% to 24.0% guided range. The market pays roughly 20x a rising earnings base as the cyclical discount fades.

scenarios.name: Base
scenarios.driver: Zebra executes to its raised full-year guidance, but organic growth stays mid-single-digit and the one-time tariff and currency benefits do not repeat. The stock holds near the consensus target as the market keeps paying a mid-to-high-teens forward multiple on a modestly rising earnings base.

scenarios.name: Bear
scenarios.driver: The enterprise-hardware cycle turns as it did in FY23, when revenue fell -20.7%. Organic demand stalls, the tariff and currency tailwinds reverse, and the multiple compresses toward 13x a flat earnings base. Elevated debt and a 0.52 current ratio amplify the derating.

valuation.scenarioCommentary: The three scenarios weight to a fair value only modestly above today's price, so the expected upside is limited while the bear case carries real downside — a reward/risk that does not clear our BUY threshold. The Base case assumes Zebra delivers its own guidance without help from the tariff refund or currency, the most likely path given a raised outlook but decelerating organic growth. The Bull case requires the cyclical discount to lift and organic growth to re-accelerate, neither of which is visible in the current organic rate. The Bear case is anchored to the company's own FY23 experience, when revenue fell more than a fifth, and is deepened by the thinner balance sheet after Elo. The probability-weighted fair value sits inside our $355 to $445 target band and near the Base implied price.

segments.name: Consolidated
segments.body: The vendor data rolls Zebra's two divisions into a single consolidated line, but the filing breaks them out. Connected Frontline — mobile computing, point-of-sale, kiosks and workflow software — posted net sales of $903 million in the quarter ended July 4, 2026, {+ up 25.9% +} from $717 million, though excluding currency and the Elo acquisition its organic growth was 7.5%. Asset Visibility & Automation — thermal printing and supplies, data capture, fixed industrial scanning, machine vision, RFID and real-time location systems — posted $654 million, up from $576 million, with faster organic growth of 11.4%. Both divisions grew across all regions, led by North America at $774 million. The mix pairs cyclical hardware with a recurring supplies-and-services stream that steadies revenue when equipment demand slows.

moatFactors.name: Scale and installed base
moatFactors.body: Zebra describes itself as a global leader in AIDC, and its installed base of mobile computers, scanners and printers across retail, logistics, manufacturing and healthcare creates a large replacement and attach-rate opportunity. Scale supports the research budget — research and development was $159 million in the quarter — needed to keep the hardware and software portfolio current.

moatFactors.name: Switching costs
moatFactors.body: Enterprise AIDC deployments are embedded in customer workflows and increasingly paired with cloud software subscriptions, which raises the cost of switching vendors mid-cycle. Services and software revenue of $241 million in the quarter reflects that ongoing attachment.

moatFactors.name: Distribution and supplies
moatFactors.body: Sales run through a direct force plus a broad channel-partner network, and a recurring supplies stream — thermal labels, ribbons, RFID tags and consumables — pulls through with the installed base and is harder for a competitor to displace than a single hardware bid.

businessMoat.durability: Zebra's moat is real but narrow. The installed base, channel network and recurring supplies-and-services revenue give the franchise staying power and some insulation when hardware demand softens. Against that, AIDC is a cyclical, competitive hardware market: revenue contracted in the FY23 downturn, and the current results are flattered by tariff recoveries, currency and the Elo acquisition rather than a durable step-change in organic demand. Automation and 'Physical AI' adoption are genuine secular tailwinds, but they have not yet shown up as double-digit organic growth. The durability case rests on Zebra defending share and converting automation demand into organic growth, not on pricing power strong enough to override the cycle.

points: Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to net sales growth of 14% to 16% and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $20.75 to $21.25, with free cash flow above $1 billion.
Third-quarter guidance is for net sales growth of 17% to 20%, including about 10.5 points from acquisitions, dispositions and currency, and non-GAAP EPS of $4.70 to $4.90.
Organic growth is the swing factor, running in the high-single digits and below the reported rate in both the quarter and year to date.
The Elo acquisition, closed September 30, 2025 for about $1.3 billion, expands the Connected Frontline segment and lifts reported growth for twelve months.
Consensus expects revenue of $6.6B and EPS of $22.20 in FY27, up from an estimated $6.2B and $21.04 in FY26.

management.leadership: William Burns is Chief Executive Officer and Nathan Winters is Chief Financial Officer, both named in the quarterly release. The broader named-executive group as of December 31, 2025 included Richard Hudson as Chief Revenue Officer and Cristen Kogl as Chief Legal Officer, General Counsel and Corporate Secretary. The team saw turnover into 2026: the former Chief Product and Solutions Officer resigned in November 2025, and the former Chief People Officer stepped down at the end of 2025 and moved to a senior advisory role ahead of a planned May 2026 retirement. Anders Gustafsson, the former CEO, has served as Chair of the Board since 2024.
management.capitalAllocation: Capital allocation tilts to buybacks and M&A rather than dividends. Zebra pays no dividend and repurchased $568 million of stock year to date through the most recent quarter, including $268 million in the quarter, after $587M in FY25. Beyond buybacks, the $1.3 billion Elo acquisition in September 2025 was the main capital outlay, lifting total debt to $2,776 million as of July 4, 2026. With guided free cash flow above $1 billion for 2026 and a capital-light model — FY25 capital expenditure was $86 million — the company has the cash flow to service that debt and keep buying back stock, but the 0.52 current ratio leaves less cushion for a downturn than the free-cash-flow headline suggests.
management.governance: Governance is conventional and shareholder-tested. Under Nasdaq rules a majority of directors must be independent, and in February 2026 the Board determined every director was independent except Chair Anders Gustafsson, the former CEO, and CEO William Burns. Because the Chair is not independent, the Board maintains a Lead Independent Director, Michael Smith, who has served in that role since 2024 and as a director since 1991. The 2025 say-on-pay vote drew 94.2% support, and the company maintains related-party, anti-hedging, clawback and interlocking-directorate policies. Corporate Governance Guidelines cap outside public-company board seats at four for non-employee directors.

idiosyncratic: Transitory earnings support: the quarter included roughly $73 million of IEEPA tariff recoveries and favorable currency that lifted gross margin 540 bps; these benefits are one-time and mask a high-single-digit organic rate.
Cyclicality: AIDC hardware demand tracks enterprise capital spending, and Zebra's own revenue fell in the FY23 downturn, so a slowdown could reverse both the growth and the margin gains quickly.

Integration and impairment: the $1.3 billion Elo acquisition added goodwill and intangibles that the FY2025 Form 10-K identifies as at risk of impairment if the business underperforms, and integration could divert management attention.
Balance-sheet thinness: total debt of $2,776 million and a 0.52 current ratio, together with rising interest expense, reduce flexibility if cash flow weakens.
Reported-versus-organic gap: with about 8 points of guided full-year growth from acquisitions and currency, headline momentum could fade as the Elo contribution laps and currency normalizes.
risks.systemic: Zebra is exposed to the broad enterprise technology spending cycle, and demand across retail, logistics, manufacturing and healthcare moves with global industrial activity. As a global company that manufactures through a contract supply chain, it is sensitive to foreign-currency swings, tariffs and trade policy — the same IEEPA tariff regime that produced this quarter's refund created the original cost — and to component costs, including memory, which management says it mitigated through price realization. Geopolitical disruption, including the conflicts and China-Taiwan tensions named in the Form 10-K, could pressure both supply and demand. None of these is unique to Zebra, but each can move a cyclical hardware franchise more than a diversified software peer.

body: We rate Zebra HOLD. This is a well-run AIDC leader with expanding margins, a raised 2026 outlook and strong free cash flow, but the quarter's headline strength leans on tariff recoveries, currency and the Elo acquisition rather than organic demand, which grew a steadier high-single-digit rate. At $367.54, near the top of its 52-week range and about 17.5x forward earnings, the shares already price continued execution.

The setup is balanced rather than compelling: our probability-weighted fair value sits only modestly above the current price and inside a $355 to $445 target band, while the bear case — anchored to Zebra's own FY23 revenue decline — carries more than 20% downside. That asymmetry keeps us from the Buy case the Street holds. What to watch is organic growth: a sustained move above the current high-single-digit rate would justify a higher multiple, while a slip back toward the mid-single digits, paired with the fading tariff and currency benefits, would expose the valuation.
